KEY MESSAGE 1...Quiet through the rest of today, cooler 
tonight, with clouds returning before sunrise.

A 1020-1025 mb high pressure system responsible for today's 
gorgeous weather drifts offshore tonight ahead of our next 
system for Sunday. Before that arrives, continued fall-like 
weather is expected this afternoon and overnight. Winds decouple
overnight, becoming fairly light to calm in some areas. In 
addition, feel the cloud cover will be slower to move in. While 
clouds push in from the west overnight, thinking these will 
initially be mainly high clouds. Thus, should still see a period
of good radiational cooling during the first part of the night,
while eastern areas of southern New England may see a majority 
of the night before clouds fully arrive.

As is typical with this setup, the NBM appears too mild, so 
have blended in the cooler MOS/MET/MAV guidance. This really 
highlights the colder pockets along the I-495 corridor, the 
hollows of northern Massachusetts, and the Vineyard. All of 
these areas fall well into the lower 40s tonight, though it is 
not out of the realm of possibility to see an upper 30 sprinkled
in there. Otherwise, urban centers such as Boston, Providence, 
and Hartford remain in the upper 40s to lower 50s. Worcester 
stays relatively mild as well, given the city's elevation and 
location near the top of the nocturnal inversion.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Briefly dry early to mid morning, then 
beneficial rain overspreads southern New England and continues 
through the evening and overnight hours. Flooding concerns 
remain low.

As advertised, conditions Sunday aren't ideal for outdoor 
activities, with a raw, cool, and rainy day expected. Highs are 
mainly in the lower to middle 60s across the coastal plain, with
middle to upper 50s across the higher elevations of southern 
New England.

A subtle mid-level northern stream trough arrives from the west
early Sunday morning, accompanied by a modest 850 mb jet, 
though the jet weakens in magnitude as it shifts east. This 
should provide enough forcing to capitalize on PWATs ranging 
from 1.4 to 1.9 inches, or roughly 150-200 percent of normal. 
Despite the anomalous moisture, we aren't concerned about 
impacts similar to those experienced with last Sunday's 
heavy/torrential rainfall and flooding. Last Sunday's event was 
considerably more convective in nature, while Sunday's rainfall 
should be predominantly stratiform. This should favor lower 
rainfall rates and greatly reduce the potential for localized 
torrential downpours that contributed to flooding last weekend.

Timing this out, widespread rain develops during the mid to 
late morning and persists well into the evening. There is pretty
good agreement among the 19/12z suite of high-res guidance. By 
18z/2 PM, rain should be widespread across much of the region. 
The exception will be the outer Cape and Nantucket, which may 
remain dry for an additional hour or two. There is some, albeit 
limited, instability near the south coast, where we cannot rule 
out a rumble of thunder and briefly heavier rainfall. One other 
area to monitor is near the Mass Pike and the transition from 
the coastal plain into the higher terrain of central 
Massachusetts. High-res guidance shows a convergence boundary 
developing in this vicinity, which may lead to a corridor of 
enhanced rainfall.

Overall, rainfall amounts of 0.5-1.0 inch are expected, though 
some variability from town to town is likely, especially near 
any areas of enhanced rainfall. The HREF maximum does show 
localized amounts approaching 2 inches, representing the upper 
end of the guidance envelope, but confidence in amounts this 
high is quite low. Given the generally lower rainfall rates, the
risk for flooding remains low. Some minor ponding is possible 
where leaves or other debris clog storm drains, but otherwise 
this should be a beneficial rainfall for the region.

With plenty of cloud cover overnight and a breezy northerly 
wind, there are no concerns for a particularly chilly night. It 
will remain raw and wet, with lows in the upper 40s to lower 
50s. Rain shifts offshore with the front early Monday morning, 
coming to an end by or before daybreak.

KEY MESSAGE 3...High pressure Tuesday gives way to a coastal 
system for the second half of the week. 

Ensemble guidance remains in good agreement that an anomolously
strong high pressure system will develop over Quebec Tuesday 
and linger into Wed/Thurs. This system likely keeps temperatures
across New England cooler than normal, in the low to mid 60s.
 
Both deterministic and ensemble guidance continue to indicate 
potential for a coastal low to form sometime Thursday into 
Friday. While there is still a large amount of uncertainty in
